title: Making the case
grammar: Formal suggestions and the subjunctive (I suggest that…, it's essential that…, it's important that he be…)

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: Make your case! Learn to write a persuasive essay, use formal suggestions and the subjunctive, and win the argument.
scene.intro: Welcome to Unit 5. Now the project needs a voice on paper. In this unit you read how to plan a persuasive essay for the exam, you learn formal suggestions and the subjunctive (it is essential that schools teach…), and you prepare for the opinion essay in Writing Part 1. A strong opinion needs a strong structure — let's build one.

activities.title: Reading — making your case in the exam

data.title: Making your case in the exam
data.author: mateo
data.text:
In the B2 First Writing paper, Part one always asks for an essay. You are given a question and two ideas, and you must argue clearly. For Inspiring Nordic, we turned this exam skill into a real one: writing to persuade our school to support the trades.

Mateo — that's me — learned the hard way that opinions are not enough. A strong essay needs structure. It is essential that every paragraph have one clear idea, supported by a reason and an example. Examiners reward organisation.

Our teacher taught us the language of emphasis. Instead of “schools should teach repair skills”, we now write, “It is vital that schools teach practical skills.” The subjunctive sounds formal and confident. Sofía suggested that we also include a counter-argument, because acknowledging the other side makes you more convincing, not less.

Nadia added a golden rule: always plan before you write. She recommends four paragraphs — an introduction, two body paragraphs and a conclusion. Liam, who used to write huge, messy answers, now sticks to the word limit.

What have we learned? A persuasive essay is not about big words; it is about clear thinking, honest reasons and a confident voice. Master that, and you can make your case — in the exam, and in the world.

activities.title: Grammar — Formal suggestions and the subjunctive

data.title: Formal suggestions and the subjunctive
data.intro: To sound formal and persuasive, we use the subjunctive after certain expressions. After 'it is essential/important/vital that' and verbs like 'suggest, recommend, propose', the verb stays in its base form for every subject.

examples.text: It is essential that every paragraph have one clear idea.
It is important that he be on time.
I suggest that she include a counter-argument.
We recommend that the school support the trades.

rules: After it is essential/important/vital that, use the base form of the verb (he be, she have).
After suggest, recommend, propose, insist that, also use the base form.
The subjunctive does not change for the third person: he be, not 'he is'; she have, not 'she has'.

items.sentence: It is essential that everyone ___ on time.
I suggest that she ___ a counter-argument.
It is vital that the school ___ practical skills.
We recommend that he ___ his plan first.
It is important that every paragraph ___ one clear idea.

activities.title: Use of English Part 2 — open cloze. Write ONE word in each gap.

data.text: A good essay is not difficult {1} you plan it well. First, decide {2} your opinion is, and write it clearly {3} the introduction. Each paragraph should have one idea {4} is supported by an example. It is essential {5} you also mention the other side. Finally, end {6} a strong conclusion.

data.voice_note: Voz: la profesora (Miss Vega), con consejos para el ensayo del examen.
data.script: Hello, Grade 10. Let's prepare for the Writing paper. In Part one you must write an essay of about one hundred and forty words. My first tip: always plan. It is essential that your essay have four paragraphs — an introduction, two main ideas, and a conclusion. Second, use formal language; avoid slang. Third, include a counter-argument to sound balanced. And remember to check your grammar at the end. Mateo will share his model essay on Wednesday. Write clearly, argue honestly, and your marks will improve.

activities.title: Speaking — making a case. In pairs, then record it.

data.text: In pairs, practise making a case. Model: “It is essential that our school support the trades, because these skills last a lifetime.” 1) Should schools spend more time on practical subjects? Give one reason for and one against. 2) Suggest, formally, one change your school should make (e.g. “I recommend that the school open a workshop.”). 3) What makes an argument convincing rather than just loud? Give reasons and examples, then record your discussion.

homework.prompt: Write a short opinion essay (about 120–150 words) answering: 'Should every student learn a practical trade?' Include an introduction, two reasons and a conclusion, and use at least three formal structures with the subjunctive (e.g. 'It is essential that schools teach…' / 'I recommend that students be…'). Capital letters and full stops!
